Where it began

Rohan Kanhai was born in Port Mourant, in what was then British Guiana, on 26 December 1935. He came into the West Indies side on the 1957 tour of England, and his start was a busy one: in his first three Tests he opened the batting and kept wicket as well, before handing the gloves to Gerry Alexander for the last two matches.

The player

He played 79 Tests from 1957 to 1974 and made 6,227 runs at 47.53, with 15 hundreds and 28 fifties. His highest score was 256, against India at Calcutta. When he finished, only four West Indians with more than 20 Tests had a better average.

Late in his career he followed Gary Sobers as captain, leading the side in 13 Tests and giving it fresh steel and purpose. Then, in 1975, grey-haired and in his 40th year, he made a calm half-century in the first World Cup final, laying the ground for a thunderous innings from Clive Lloyd. The West Indies won the trophy without losing a match.

What made him special

He played shots nobody else would have tried. The most famous was the falling hook, after which he often ended up flat on his back watching the ball sail away. It was on show at The Oval in 1963, during an innings of 77 that won the match. The writer C. L. R. James saw in him the summit of West Indian cricket and loved his sense of adventure.

All that boldness carried some risk, of course, and a batsman who finishes a shot lying on the grass gives bowlers a little hope. They rarely got much else from him.

Away from the middle

He played all over the world, for Guyana, Trinidad, Tasmania and Western Australia among others, but England knew him best. For Warwickshire he made 11,615 first-class runs at 51.62, figures few batsmen there have matched over so long a stay. Before that, in the 1963–64 season, he helped Ashington in Northumberland win both their league and their cup, and big crowds came to watch.

In 1992 he became the first national coach of the West Indies, working with the under-19s before taking on the Test side, until 1995. Wisden made him a Cricketer of the Year, and in 2009 he joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame.

And finally

Sunil Gavaskar thought him the greatest batsman he had ever seen, and showed it by naming his son Rohan. The Australian spinner Bob Holland did the same. Ashington chose a different tribute: a pub in the town carries his name.
